lesson.title: Which way will molecules move?

steps.headline: Diffusion is the net movement of a substance from where it is crowded to where it is not.

lead.text: A solute is a dissolved substance. Its particles move at random, so some cross a gap each way. More particles cross from the crowded side, and the difference is the net movement.
When concentrations are equal, the flows match. That balance is equilibrium.
Here is the same idea on a membrane. Compare how crowded each side is, then think about which way more particles cross.

reveal.text: You predicted the direction of net movement: from the more concentrated side to the less concentrated side. Individual particles still cross both ways.

steps.headline: Equal volumes hold 9 and 3 units of freely crossing solute. How many units are on each side at equilibrium?

workedSteps.text: Solute only moves, so the total is fixed.
Then split it between two equal volumes.

steps.headline: Equal volumes hold 10 and 6 units. How many are on each side at equilibrium?

workedSteps.text: Share the total between the two equal volumes.

steps.headline: A membrane only passes the substances it is permeable to.

lead.text: Membranes are selective. A membrane is permeable to a substance if that substance can cross it, and impermeable if it cannot.
Always check this before you predict any movement.
Compare the two cases on the screen. Ask what can cross in each before you follow any difference in concentration.

reveal.text: You checked permeability before following the gradient. When a substance cannot cross, the difference in concentration moves nothing.

lead.text: At equilibrium nothing seems to change. Yet particles keep crossing, in both directions, at the same average rate.

reveal.text: Equal concentrations mean no net movement, not no solute. Diffusion moves solute around and never destroys it.

lesson.orientation: Predict net diffusion from concentration and membrane permeability.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Two equal rooms are joined by an open door. 20 people stand in the left room and 4 in the right.
Everyone wanders at random, in any direction, through the door.

intro.promise: By the end you'll predict which way a dissolved substance moves across a membrane, and when it will not move at all.
intro.whyItMatters: It explains how cells take in nutrients without spending energy.

recap.keyIdea: A solute that can cross a membrane moves net from the crowded side to the sparse side until the concentrations match. A solute that cannot cross stays put.

blocks.text: You shared 24 people between two equal rooms and 16 solute units between two equal compartments. The totals did not change. A blocked solute kept its starting amount.

recap.nextHook: Water can cross a membrane that solute cannot. Which way does the water go?

questions.prompt: Equal volumes hold 12 solute units on the left and 4 on the right, and solute can cross. In which direction is there net movement at first?
hints: Which side is more concentrated? Compare amounts, since the volumes are equal.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The left side is more concentrated, so net solute movement is to the right.

questions.onCorrect: Left to right: from the more concentrated side to the less concentrated side.

misconceptions.feedback: That runs from the sparser side to the crowded one. Net movement goes the other way.
The two sides differ in concentration, so more particles cross one way than the other.

questions.prompt: Two fixed equal volumes contain 10 and 6 units of freely crossing solute. How many units are on each side at equilibrium?
hints: Keep the total solute constant.
Add the amounts on the two sides.
Divide the total between two equal volumes.
questions.onCorrect: 8 each. Total solute stays constant, and equal volumes finish with equal amounts.

misconceptions.feedback: That's both sides together. Share it between the two compartments.
That's the left side's starting amount. Some of it has moved across.

questions.prompt: 12 solute units start on the left and 4 on the right. The barrier blocks both solute and water. How many solute units are on the left after a long time?
hints: Check what can cross first.
If nothing can cross, can any amount change?
Each side keeps the amount it started with.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Nothing can cross, so each side keeps its starting amount: 12 on the left.

questions.onCorrect: 12. A barrier that blocks the solute leaves the amounts unchanged, whatever the difference in concentration.

misconceptions.feedback: That would need solute to cross, and this barrier blocks it.
That's the right side's amount. Ask about the left side.

questions.prompt: At equal concentration, 8 units are on each side. How many solute units are in the whole two-compartment system?
hints: Count both compartments.
There are eight units in each.
Add the two equal amounts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 8 + 8 = 16 units. Diffusion does not destroy solute.

questions.onCorrect: 16. Equilibrium means equal concentrations, not missing solute: the total is unchanged.

misconceptions.feedback: That's one side. Count both compartments.

questions.prompt: At diffusion equilibrium, which statement is accurate?
hints: Separate no net change from no motion.

acceptedIdeas: Molecules cross both ways with no net flow
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Equilibrium is dynamic: opposite flows balance on average.

choices.label: Molecules cross both ways with no net flow
All molecules move in one direction

questions.onCorrect: Particles keep crossing both ways at equal rates, so there is no net flow.

misconceptions.feedback: Particles keep moving. What stops is the net change in concentration.
One-way movement would keep changing the concentrations. At equilibrium the flows balance.

questions.prompt: A separate equal-volume system starts with 14 solute units on one side and 2 on the other. How many units must move net from the concentrated side to reach equilibrium?
hints: Find the equilibrium amount first.
The total is shared between two equal volumes.
Subtract the equilibrium amount from the starting amount on the crowded side.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each side finishes with 8. The concentrated side loses 14 − 8 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Find the equal share first, then see how far the crowded side must fall to reach it.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the amount each side ends with. How many had to move to get there?
That's the gap between the sides. Only half of the gap has to cross.

questions.prompt: A membrane is permeable to water but not to a dye. 9 dye units are on the left and 3 on the right. How many dye units are on the left after a long time?
hints: Which substances can cross this membrane?
Can the dye cross?
If the dye cannot move, its amounts stay as they began.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The dye cannot cross, so its amounts do not change: 9 on the left.

questions.onCorrect: 9. The dye cannot cross, so a concentration difference moves nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what each side would hold if the dye could cross. Check what the membrane lets through.
That's the right side's amount. Ask about the left.

questions.prompt: After a long time, how many people are in the left room?
hints: Does anyone leave the building, or arrive?
Count everyone in both rooms together.
Think about sharing that crowd between two equal rooms.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Everyone is still in the building: 20 + 4 = 24. Equal rooms end up with equal crowds: 24 ÷ 2 = 12.

questions.onCorrect: 12. People cross both ways, but more leave the crowded room, so the rooms settle at equal numbers.

misconceptions.feedback: That's where the left room started. People keep crossing the door, so the count changes.
That's everyone in the building. The question asks about the left room only.

questions.prompt: Dye is dropped into still water. Overall, where does the dye move?
hints: Which region sends more particles across the boundary between them?

acceptedIdeas: From where it is crowded to where it is not
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Net movement runs from the more concentrated region to the less concentrated one.

choices.label: From where it is crowded to where it is not
From where it is sparse to where it is crowded

questions.onCorrect: From crowded to sparse. More particles cross that way, so the net movement follows.

misconceptions.feedback: That would make the crowd even more crowded. More particles leave the crowded region than enter it.
Particles move constantly. It is the net movement that settles down, not the particles.

questions.prompt: Why does the total stay the same while solute moves?
hints: Think about where each particle goes.

acceptedIdeas: Solute only moves from place to place; none is made or lost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Diffusion moves solute between compartments but does not create or destroy it.

choices.label: Solute only moves from place to place; none is made or lost
Solute is replaced from outside the compartments
The two sides swap their solute exactly

questions.onCorrect: Diffusion only moves solute around. The total is conserved, so you can add the sides first.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing arrives from outside this closed system.
The sides don't swap. Net movement stops once the concentrations match.

questions.prompt: What word describes a membrane that lets a substance cross?
hints: The word starts with per-, meaning through.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A membrane is permeable to a substance if the substance can cross it.

questions.onCorrect: Permeable. Always check what a membrane is permeable to before predicting movement.

misconceptions.feedback: Impermeable means the opposite: nothing can cross.

Random movement in both directions produces net movement from crowded to sparse and then equilibrium.
